power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Direction of apoB/LDL-C Discordance and Systemic Inflammation in U.S. Adults

author.affiliation:
Department of Internal Medicine
								St. Elizabeth Youngstown Hospital
								
									Youngstown
									OH

text.text: Background: Apolipoprotein B (apoB) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) are established biomarkers of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) that tend to be closely correlated.

However, some individuals have discordant apoB and LDL-C. We evaluated whether apoB/LDL-C discordance is associated with elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), a key marker of systemic inflammation, in a nationally representative sample.

We analyzed cross-sectional data of 2226 adults aged 20 years or older from the 2015 to 2016 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey with complete apoB, LDL-C, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP).
LDL-C and apoB were converted to surveyweighted scores, and discordance was the residual of apoB regressed on LDL-C. Participants were classified as apoB-high, LDL-C-high, or concordant (reference).
The association of discordance group with elevated hs-CRP (>3 mg/L) was estimated with survey-weighted logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, body mass index (BMI), and diabetes.
text.formatted: The association of discordance group with elevated hs-CRP (>3 mg/L) was estimated with survey-weighted logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, body mass index (BMI), and diabetes.

text.text: Discordance was present in 26.4% of adults (13.7% apoB-higher, 12.6% LDL-C-higher).

Elevated hs-CRP prevalence differed by discordance group: 47.6% (95% CI, 37.6-57.7) in the apoB-high group versus 20.5% (12.9-28.1) in the LDL-C-high group and 33.6% (29.7-37.4) in the concordant group.

Relative to concordant participants, adjusted odds of elevated hs-CRP were higher for apoB-high discordance (odds ratio [OR], 1.58; 95% CI, 1.03-2.45) and lower for LDL-C-high discordance (OR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.30-0.78).
Similar results were obtained among participants not on statin therapy, with apoB-high discordance demonstrating stronger adjusted odds of elevated hs-CRP (OR, 2.02; 95% CI, 1.01-4.04).
Conclusion: Discordantly high apoB relative to LDL-C is associated with systemic inflammation in a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults.

Lowering LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) is central to the prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), and LDL-C remains the principal target of lipid-lowering guidelines worldwide [1] [2] [3].
text.formatted: Lowering LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) is central to the prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), and LDL-C remains the principal target of lipid-lowering guidelines worldwide <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: The causal role of LDL and other apolipoprotein B (apoB)-containing lipoproteins in atherogenesis is supported by genetic, epidemiologic, and clinical trial evidence [4].
text.formatted: The causal role of LDL and other apolipoprotein B (apoB)-containing lipoproteins in atherogenesis is supported by genetic, epidemiologic, and clinical trial evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: However, LDL-C quantifies the cholesterol mass carried within circulating lipoproteins, not the number of atherogenic particles.

Because each atherogenic lipoprotein, including very-low-density lipoprotein, intermediate-density lipoprotein, LDL, and lipoprotein(a), carries a single apoB molecule, apoB provides a direct count of the atherogenic particle burden [5, 6].
text.formatted: Because each atherogenic lipoprotein, including very-low-density lipoprotein, intermediate-density lipoprotein, LDL, and lipoprotein(a), carries a single apoB molecule, apoB provides a direct count of the atherogenic particle burden <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6]</ref>.

text.text: When cholesterol mass and particle number diverge, LDL-C and apoB become discordant [5].
text.formatted: When cholesterol mass and particle number diverge, LDL-C and apoB become discordant <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Multiple cohorts have shown that when apoB and LDL-C disagree, cardiovascular risk tracks with apoB rather than with LDL-C, and that discordant elevation of apoB predicts incident events and subclinical atherosclerosis beyond LDL-C [5, [7] [8] [9].
text.formatted: Multiple cohorts have shown that when apoB and LDL-C disagree, cardiovascular risk tracks with apoB rather than with LDL-C, and that discordant elevation of apoB predicts incident events and subclinical atherosclerosis beyond LDL-C <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: These observations have contributed to the incorporation of apoB into clinical guidelines as a risk-enhancing factor and an alternative measure of atherogenic burden [2, 3].
text.formatted: These observations have contributed to the incorporation of apoB into clinical guidelines as a risk-enhancing factor and an alternative measure of atherogenic burden <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3]</ref>.

text.text: Recent nationally representative data indicate that apoB/LDL-C discordance is common in the general population [10].
text.formatted: Recent nationally representative data indicate that apoB/LDL-C discordance is common in the general population <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: In parallel, systemic inflammation has emerged as an independent and modifiable contributor to ASCVD [11].
text.formatted: In parallel, systemic inflammation has emerged as an independent and modifiable contributor to ASCVD <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) is a validated marker of inflammatory risk that predicts cardiovascular events across the spectrum of LDL-C [12] [13] [14], and an hs-CRP concentration greater than 3 mg/L identifies individuals at higher vascular risk [12].
text.formatted: High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) is a validated marker of inflammatory risk that predicts cardiovascular events across the spectrum of LDL-C <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>, and an hs-CRP concentration greater than 3 mg/L identifies individuals at higher vascular risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Antiinflammatory therapy reduces cardiovascular events independent of lipid lowering [15] [16] [17], and among statin-treated patients, inflammation assessed by hs-CRP predicts residual risk at least as strongly as LDL-C [18].
text.formatted: Antiinflammatory therapy reduces cardiovascular events independent of lipid lowering <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>, and among statin-treated patients, inflammation assessed by hs-CRP predicts residual risk at least as strongly as LDL-C <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: A 2025 American College of Cardiology Scientific Statement summarizes the growing evidence base linking inflammation to cardiovascular disease and its assessment in clinical care [19].
text.formatted: A 2025 American College of Cardiology Scientific Statement summarizes the growing evidence base linking inflammation to cardiovascular disease and its assessment in clinical care <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: The metabolic profile that produces an elevation of apoB relative to LDL-C may also promote inflammation.

Remnant and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins have been linked to causing cause lowgrade inflammation [20, 21], so it is plausible that the direction of apoB/LDL-C discordance (more specifically, apoB-high discordance) carries information about concurrent inflammation.
text.formatted: Remnant and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins have been linked to causing cause lowgrade inflammation <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21]</ref>, so it is plausible that the direction of apoB/LDL-C discordance (more specifically, apoB-high discordance) carries information about concurrent inflammation.

text.text: Previ-ous discordance research has focused on atherosclerotic events and subclinical disease rather than inflammatory burden, and it has not been examined whether discordance is associated with lowgrade inflammation in the general population.

We used the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) to determine whether the direction of apoB/LDL-C discordance is associated with low-grade systemic inflammation among U.S. adults, and to examine the extent to which adiposity and sex account for that association.
NHANES data are publicly available from the National Center for Health Statistics [22].
text.formatted: NHANES data are publicly available from the National Center for Health Statistics <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: Analytic code will be made available upon reasonable request.
We analyzed the 2015-2016 cycle of NHANES, a continuous, cross-sectional survey of the civilian noninstitutionalized US population that uses a complex, multistage probability sampling design.
Details of recruitment, examination, and laboratory procedures are described elsewhere [23].
text.formatted: Details of recruitment, examination, and laboratory procedures are described elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: Note that the 2015-2016 cycle is the only NHANES cycle with concurrent measurements of both apoB and hs-CRP.
The analytic sample comprised adults aged 20 years or older with complete data for apoB, LDL-C, hs-CRP, and survey design variables.
Because apoB and calculated LDL-C were measured in the morning fasting subsample, eligibility required participation in that subsample.
The participant flowchart is shown in Figure 1.
text.formatted: The participant flowchart is shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: The final analytic sample included 2,226 participants.
Adjusted models were restricted to the 2,151 participants with complete covariate data.
apoB was measured by immunoturbidimetric assay and hs-CRP by particle immunoassay on automated analyzers.
LDL-C was the NHANES-provided value calculated using the Friedewald equation.
Full laboratory methods are available in the NHANES documentation [22].
text.formatted: Full laboratory methods are available in the NHANES documentation <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: There is no universally accepted definition of discordance in the literature.
Existing approaches fall into three broad classes: cut points [10, 24], population percentiles [25], and regression residuals [26, 27].
text.formatted: Existing approaches fall into three broad classes: cut points <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24]</ref>, population percentiles <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>, and regression residuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27]</ref>.

text.text: We adopt the residual-based approach here: LDL-C and apoB were each converted to survey-weighted scores using the weighted mean and standard deviation, and the apoB score was regressed on the LDL-C score.
Because both variables were standardized, the slope equals the weighted correlation ( ), and the expected apoB score for a given LDL-C score is times the LDL-C score.
The residual (observed minus expected apoB score) was divided by its expected standard deviation, √ 1 -2 , to yield a residual discordance score, , on an interpretable scale.
Participants were classified using an absolute residual discordance score threshold of 1: • apoB higher than LDL-C: ≥ +1 • LDL-C higher than apoB: ≤ -1
This method asks whether a participant's apoB is higher or lower than expected given the participant's LDL-C.

The outcome was elevated hs-CRP, defined as an hs-CRP concentration greater than 3 mg/L, consistent with the American Heart Association and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention threshold for higher relative vascular risk [12].
text.formatted: The outcome was elevated hs-CRP, defined as an hs-CRP concentration greater than 3 mg/L, consistent with the American Heart Association and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention threshold for higher relative vascular risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Analyses were conducted in R using the survey package.
Because apoB and calculated LDL-C are measured in the morning fasting subsample, all estimates used the NHANES fasting subsample 2-year sampling weights (WTSAF2YR).

The primary analysis was a logistic regression model with elevated hs-CRP as the dependent variable and discordance group as the independent variable, entered as two indicator terms with the concordant group as the reference.
We report an unadjusted model and a model adjusted for age, sex, BMI, and diagnosed diabetes.

To identify which covariates accounted for the change in the adjusted estimates, we fit a sequence of nested models on a single fixed sample of participants with complete covariate data, adding covariates one at a time.
Holding the sample constant ensures that any change in the odds ratio reflects the covariate added rather than a change in sample composition.
A two-sided value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

In a prespecified sensitivity analysis, we repeated the unadjusted and adjusted models after excluding participants taking a statin (atorvastatin, simvastatin, rosuvastatin, pravastatin, lovastatin, fluvastatin, or pitavastatin).
The mean LDL-C was 112.6 (SD 35.7) mg/dL and mean apoB was 93.2 (SD 25.5) mg/dL.
A scatter plot of the weighted apoB z score versus LDL-C z score is shown in Fig. 2.

The overall survey-weighted prevalence of elevated hs-CRP was 33.8% (95% CI, 29.8-37.9).

text.text: The three discordance groups differed in cardiometabolic profile.

Compared with the concordant group, the apoB-high group had higher BMI (31.5 versus 29.3 kg/m 2 ), a greater proportion of diagnosed diabetes (30.0% versus 8.8%), older mean age (53.2 versus 47.3 years), and a higher proportion of men (56.7% versus 48.0%).

The LDL-C-high group had the most favorable profile on these measures, including the lowest BMI (28.0 kg/m 2 ), lowest diabetes prevalence (1.9%), youngest mean age (42.2 years), and lowest proportion of men (37.4%). apoB/LDL-C discordance was present in 26.4% of adults at the absolute residual score threshold of 1, with the two directions of similar frequency: 13.7% had apoB higher than LDL-C and 12.6% had LDL-C higher than apoB; the remaining 73.6% were concordant (Table 2).

In the unadjusted model, the odds of elevated hs-CRP were higher for apoB-high discordance (OR, 1.80; 95% CI, 1.21-2.67; = 0.006) and lower for LDL-C-higher discordance (OR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.32-0.81; = 0.007) (Table 3) relative to concordant participants.

text.text: Starting from the crude estimate ( = 1.82), adding BMI dropped the odds ratio to 1.50, whereas further adding sex raised it back to 1.62.
Age and diabetes had minimal impact.
We can understand these opposing shifts by examining the participant profiles.
Participants in the apoB-high group had a higher average BMI than the reference group (31.5 vs.
Because higher BMI correlates with elevated hs-CRP, adjusting for BMI removed positive confounding and lowered the odds ratio.
Conversely, the apoB-high group had a larger proportion of men (56.7% vs.
48.0%), and men were much less likely to have elevated hs-CRP than women (27.2% vs.
This surplus of lower-CRP men artificially attenuated the crude odds ratio, and adjusting for sex removed this artifact.
Since statin therapy can significantly reduce both LDL-C and hs-CRP, we conducted a sensitivity analysis to exclude participants on statins.
As seen in Table 1, statin use differed significantly across groups.
text.formatted: As seen in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, statin use differed significantly across groups.

text.text: 41.1% of the apoB-higher group were taking a statin, compared with 16.9% of the concordant group and 4.5% of the LDL-C-higher group.
This gradient is expected because statins lower LDL-C proportionally more than apoB [5, 28] and therefore shift statin-treated patients toward discordantly high apoB.

text.text: Because statins also lower hs-CRP, their concentration in the apoB-high group could further obscure the observed association.
To address the effect of statins, we repeated the analysis among statin-naive participants ( = 1,753; adjusted model = 1,711).
Notably, the pattern persisted and even strengthened in the apoB-higher group.

Compared to concordant participants, those with apoB-higher discordance had higher odds of elevated hs-CRP (crude OR, 2.38; 95% CI, 1.41-4.00; adjusted OR, 2.02; 95% CI, 1.01-4.04) and lower for LDL-C-higher discordance (adjusted OR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.28-0.81).
This stronger association aligns with our expectation.
Because statin users cluster in the apoB-high group and have pharmacologically lowered hs-CRP, including them in the full sample biases the apoB-higher association toward the null.
Excluding participants on statins removes this masking effect and offers a cleaner, though less precise (due to reduced sample size) estimate.

apoB elevation relative to LDL-C reflects an excess of cholesterol-depleted particles such as small dense LDL and remnant lipoproteins [5, 7].

text.text: Elevated remnant cholesterol has been linked to lowgrade inflammation, [20, 21], and it is plausible that individuals with discordantly high apoB carry more of these inflammation-promoting lipoproteins.
text.formatted: Elevated remnant cholesterol has been linked to lowgrade inflammation, <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21]</ref>, and it is plausible that individuals with discordantly high apoB carry more of these inflammation-promoting lipoproteins.

text.text: Our results are consistent with this account by showing that individuals with discordantly high apoB also exhibited greater inflammatory burden.
Prior discordance studies have primarily related apoB elevation to atherosclerotic events and subclinical atherosclerosis [7] [8] [9] 29].
text.formatted: Prior discordance studies have primarily related apoB elevation to atherosclerotic events and subclinical atherosclerosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29]</ref>.

text.text: By using elevated hs-CRP as the outcome, we show that high apoB relative to LDL-C identifies individuals with a substantially higher burden of systemic inflammation, whereas discordantly high LDL-C relative to apoB identifies individuals with a lower burden of chronic inflammation.
This suggests concurrent low-grade inflammation as a candidate mechanism accompanying the excess risk previously attributed to discordant apoB.
An observation of our analysis is the opposing influence of adiposity and sex.
BMI functioned as a positive confounder.
Because the apoB-high group had a higher mean BMI and adiposity drives hs-CRP, adjusting for BMI attenuated the association.
Conversely, sex acted as a suppressor variable.

The apoB-higher group was predominantly male, and since men tend to have lower hs-CRP than women [30, 31], controlling for sex strengthened the association between apoB-high discordance and elevated hs-CRP.
text.formatted: The apoB-higher group was predominantly male, and since men tend to have lower hs-CRP than women <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31]</ref>, controlling for sex strengthened the association between apoB-high discordance and elevated hs-CRP.

text.text: We consider the effect of statin therapy on our analysis.
In Table 1, we showed that statin use differed significantly across the groups, from 4.5% in the LDL-C-high group to 41.1% in the apoBhigher group.
text.formatted: In Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, we showed that statin use differed significantly across the groups, from 4.5% in the LDL-C-high group to 41.1% in the apoBhigher group.

text.text: This pattern is expected because statins lower LDL-C more effectively than apoB [5, 28], ultimately producing a relative excess of individuals with elevated apoB relative to LDL-C.
text.formatted: This pattern is expected because statins lower LDL-C more effectively than apoB <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28]</ref>, ultimately producing a relative excess of individuals with elevated apoB relative to LDL-C.

text.text: As a result of this concentration of statin users in the apoB-high group (who also are expected to have reduced hs-CRP from statin therapy), the association of apoB-high discordance with elevated inflammation was weakened.
Therefore, the full-sample estimate is biased toward the null, and the association is in fact larger among statin-naive participants (adjusted OR, 2.02 versus 1.58).
Our findings may have clinical relevance.

In patients whose apoB exceeds expectations set by LDL-C, residual cholesterol risk and inflammatory risk may coexist, thus identifying individuals for whom both particle-directed and inflammation-directed strategies could be considered.

Anti-inflammatory therapies reduce cardiovascular events [15] [16] [17], and inflammation assessed by hs-CRP predicts residual risk in treated patients [18], so recognizing an inflammation-associated lipoprotein phenotype could inform risk stratification.

text.text: Lastly, by showing that elevated hs-CRP aligns with discordantly high apoB, our findings support existing literature indicating that apoB captures cardiovascular risk more completely than LDL-C [7].
text.formatted: Lastly, by showing that elevated hs-CRP aligns with discordantly high apoB, our findings support existing literature indicating that apoB captures cardiovascular risk more completely than LDL-C <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: This study has a few limitations.
First, the design is cross-sectional and based on a single NHANES cycle, so we cannot infer whether discordantly high apoB causes low-grade inflammation or vice versa.
Secondly, estimates produced here may not generalize to other periods or populations.
Furthermore, hs-CRP was measured once, and a single measurement is subject to variation.

Finally, discordance was defined statistically from the joint distribution of apoB and LDL-C in this sample rather than by a clinical standard, and the threshold of an absolute residual score of 1 is a convention.
In a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults, the direction of apoB/LDL-C discordance was associated with systemic inflammation.
Discordantly high apoB relative to LDL-C was associated with higher odds of elevated hs-CRP, while discordantly high LDL-C relative to apoB was associated with lower odds.
These associations persisted after adjustment for age, sex, BMI, and diabetes, and the apoB-high association was stronger among statin-naive adults.
Discordantly high apoB may therefore mark a phenotype in which excess atherogenic particle burden and low-grade inflammation coexist.

Prospective studies are needed to determine whether this combination explains the excess cardiovascular risk linked to apoB-high discordance and whether it identifies patients who would benefit from both particle-lowering and anti-inflammatory therapy.
